items.locator: Normal hemodynamic values: resting adult cardiac output is generally about 4-8 L/min, average near 5 L/min; cardiac index normalizes cardiac output to body-surface area.
items.version: Current StatPearls/NCBI Bookshelf Cardiac Index entry live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: A critically ill adult has a measured cardiac output of 2.1 L/min at rest. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.A: It is above the usual resting adult range.
options.B: It is below the usual resting adult range and should be interpreted with cardiac index and perfusion findings.
options.C: It is the expected resting value for all adults.
options.D: It is normal only during exercise.

items.rationale: Resting adult cardiac output is generally about 4-8 L/min, with an average near 5 L/min. A value of 2.1 L/min is below that usual range. Option B is correct and appropriately notes that body size, cardiac index, perfusion findings, and clinical context matter. The other options misstate normal physiology.
items.finding: Fresh audit removed length-balancing padding and corrected difficulty to easy because the item is direct range interpretation.

items.source_name: AARC — Clinical Practice Guideline: Artificial Airway Suctioning (2022)
items.locator: Artificial Airway Suctioning guideline recommendations: suction only when indicated; preoxygenate adult/pediatric patients as appropriate; use sterile technique for open suctioning; generally avoid routine saline; limit suction application to a maximum of 15 seconds; use deep suction only if shallow suction is ineffective.
items.version: 2022 AARC Artificial Airway Suctioning guideline remains an active evidence-based guideline on the AARC site; currentness live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: A nurse is suctioning an adult client through an artificial airway. Which technique is consistent with current AARC guidance?

options.A: Apply suction while advancing the catheter and continue for 30 seconds.
options.B: Preoxygenate as indicated and limit each suction application to no more than about 15 seconds.
options.C: Instill normal saline routinely before every suction pass.
options.D: Perform scheduled deep suctioning even when no clinical indication is present.

items.rationale: AARC recommends preoxygenation as indicated and limiting suction application to a maximum of 15 seconds. It generally advises against routine saline instillation, favors suctioning when indicated rather than on a fixed schedule, and reserves deep suctioning for cases in which shallow suction is ineffective. Option B is correct.
items.finding: Fresh audit narrowed the keyed technique to two directly guideline-supported actions and retained only one unambiguously correct choice.

items.source_name: StatPearls/NCBI Bookshelf — Care of a Chest Tube
items.locator: Chest drainage management: keep the drainage system upright and below chest/insertion-site level to facilitate dependent drainage and prevent backflow; avoid unnecessary clamping and dependent tubing loops.
items.version: Current NCBI Bookshelf chest-tube care entry live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: Which action is appropriate for a client with a chest tube connected to a drainage system?

options.A: Place the drainage system on the bed at chest level.
options.B: Keep the drainage system upright and below the client's chest.
options.C: Raise the system above the chest during repositioning.
options.D: Clamp the tube routinely during transport.

items.rationale: Keeping the chest drainage system upright and below the chest supports drainage and reduces the risk of fluid backflow. Option B is correct. Placing the system at or above chest level or routinely clamping the tube can create complications.
items.finding: Fresh audit removed explanatory padding and corrected the blueprint to Reduction of Risk Potential because the item tests device management to prevent complications.

items.locator: Maintenance recommendations: maintain a closed drainage system and unobstructed urine flow; keep catheter/tubing free of kinks; keep the collection bag below bladder level and off the floor; do not change catheters/bags at routine fixed intervals.
items.stem: Which intervention is most important for maintaining an indwelling urinary catheter drainage system and reducing CAUTI risk?

options.A: Disconnect the catheter from the tubing once per shift for cleaning.
options.B: Rest the collection bag on the floor so it stays below the bladder.
options.C: Maintain a closed system with kink-free tubing and keep the bag below the bladder and off the floor.
options.D: Replace the catheter and bag every day even when the system is intact.

items.rationale: CDC recommends a closed drainage system with unobstructed flow, kink-free tubing, and a collection bag kept below bladder level without touching the floor. Option C is correct. Routine disconnection, floor placement, and fixed daily replacement increase risk or contradict guideline recommendations.
items.finding: Fresh audit kept the primary CDC source and removed rationale-like padding from all alternatives.

items.source_name: NCBI Bookshelf — Nursing Skills: Aseptic Technique and Wound Care
items.locator: Aseptic sequencing/wound care: proceed from clean to dirty, moving from least contaminated toward more contaminated areas and avoiding transfer of organisms back toward cleaner tissue; use clean/sterile supplies appropriately.
items.version: Current NCBI Bookshelf Nursing Skills wound-care content live-rechecked 2026-08-15; CDC sources were checked and do not provide a more specific clean-to-dirty wound-sequencing statement.
items.stem: During aseptic wound care involving areas with different contamination levels, which sequence is appropriate?

options.A: Move from the most contaminated area back toward cleaner tissue.
options.B: Use the same swab repeatedly from dirty to clean areas.
options.C: Clean in random order as long as gloves are worn.
options.D: Work from the least contaminated area toward the more contaminated area without returning used material to cleaner tissue.

items.rationale: Aseptic wound-care sequencing follows a clean-to-dirty principle: begin with the least contaminated area and move toward more contaminated areas without carrying organisms back to cleaner tissue. Option D is correct. A and B reverse that principle, and C ignores contamination control.
items.finding: Fresh audit documented that no sufficiently specific CDC wound-sequencing statement was found and therefore used the authoritative NCBI nursing-skills source per the source hierarchy's secondary-source exception.

items.source_name: CDC — HPV Vaccine Recommendations / Preventing HPV-Associated Cancers
items.locator: HPV vaccination guidance: vaccination prevents new HPV infections and works best before exposure; it does not treat existing HPV infection or disease. Routine vaccination is recommended at ages 11-12 (can start at 9), with catch-up through age 26 if not adequately vaccinated.
items.version: Current CDC HPV vaccine recommendations live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: Which statement about human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination is accurate?

options.A: It treats established HPV infection and removes existing lesions.
options.B: It prevents new infections with vaccine HPV types and works best before exposure.
options.C: It should begin only after sexual activity starts.
options.D: It eliminates the need for recommended cervical cancer screening.

items.rationale: HPV vaccination prevents new HPV infections and is most effective before exposure. It does not treat established infection or existing lesions and does not eliminate recommended screening. Option B is correct. C incorrectly delays vaccination until after exposure is more likely.
items.finding: Fresh audit removed padded teaching statements and retained current CDC prevention—not treatment—guidance.

items.locator: Recommendation Summary: screen average-risk asymptomatic adults age 45-49 (Grade B) and age 50-75 (Grade A); selectively offer screening age 76-85 based on health, prior screening, and preferences.
items.version: USPSTF Final Recommendation Statement dated 2021-05-18; remains the current final USPSTF colorectal-cancer screening recommendation, live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: An asymptomatic 45-year-old adult at average risk for colorectal cancer has never been screened. What does the USPSTF recommend?

options.B: Screen only if gastrointestinal symptoms develop.
options.C: Begin colorectal cancer screening now using an appropriate recommended strategy.

items.rationale: USPSTF recommends colorectal cancer screening beginning at age 45 for average-risk asymptomatic adults. Option C is correct. Screening is preventive rather than symptom-triggered, and multiple strategies are acceptable; annual colonoscopy is not the recommended schedule.
items.finding: Fresh audit verified that the 2021 final recommendation remains current on the USPSTF site in 2026 and removed option padding.

items.source_name: USPSTF — Intimate Partner Violence and Caregiver Abuse: Screening
items.locator: 2025 recommendation: screen women of reproductive age, including pregnant and postpartum persons, for IPV and provide or refer those who screen positive to multicomponent interventions with ongoing support; a brief referral alone is not equivalent to the evidence-supported intervention.
items.version: USPSTF Final Recommendation Statement dated 2025-06-24; currentness live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: A woman of reproductive age screens positive for intimate partner violence and is not in immediate danger. Which follow-up best reflects current USPSTF evidence?

options.A: Provide only a telephone number and end the encounter.
options.B: Require immediate separation from the partner regardless of her preferences.
options.C: Offer or refer her to a multicomponent intervention with ongoing support and address safety and resources privately.
options.D: Take no further action unless visible physical injury is present.

items.rationale: USPSTF finds benefit when women of reproductive age who screen positive for IPV are provided or referred to multicomponent interventions with ongoing support. Option C is correct and allows private safety/resource planning while respecting autonomy. A is too limited, B overrides patient choice, and D ignores a positive screen.
items.finding: Fresh audit retained the 2025 primary federal recommendation and explicitly corrected the unsupported idea that a one-time referral alone is the evidence-based intervention.

items.source_name: American Psychiatric Association — Prolonged Grief Disorder
items.locator: Symptoms and Diagnosis: persistent intense longing and/or preoccupation with the deceased with significant distress or functional impairment; for adults the death must have occurred at least one year earlier, and diagnosis requires the full DSM-5-TR criteria with cultural context considered.
items.version: APA page physician-reviewed August 2025; DSM-5-TR (2022) remains current and includes prolonged grief disorder; live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: An adult's spouse died 14 months ago. The client has persistent intense longing, preoccupation with the death, and major impairment in daily functioning. Which condition should be evaluated?
items.rationale: For adults, prolonged grief disorder is considered when a close person's death occurred at least 12 months earlier and persistent longing or preoccupation is associated with significant distress or functional impairment. Option B is the condition to evaluate; the full DSM-5-TR criteria and cultural context must still be assessed. The other choices do not fit this persistent bereavement pattern.
items.finding: Fresh audit verified the current DSM-5-TR term and 12-month adult threshold against APA's physician-reviewed August 2025 guidance and preserved 'evaluate' rather than making a diagnosis from the stem alone.

items.locator: Psychosocial Integrity activity statements/content examples: establish therapeutic relationships using therapeutic communication, support client coping and psychosocial needs, and maintain professional boundaries while providing client-centered care.
items.version: 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: Which nursing action best demonstrates therapeutic use of self in a mental health setting?

options.A: Share extensive personal experiences so the relationship becomes a friendship.
options.B: Remain emotionally detached and avoid reflecting on personal reactions.
options.C: Use self-awareness, presence, empathy, therapeutic communication, and professional boundaries to support the client's goals.
options.D: Agree with all client beliefs to maintain rapport.

items.rationale: Therapeutic use of self involves intentional, self-aware use of presence, empathy, communication, and professional boundaries to support the client's therapeutic goals. Option C is correct. Extensive self-disclosure, emotional detachment, and indiscriminate agreement undermine the therapeutic relationship.
items.finding: Fresh audit replaced a secondary literature source with the mandatory NCSBN Psychosocial Integrity framework and removed padded distractors.
